name: Road to Legend
tagline: Companion app that plays the Overlord for Descent: Journeys in the Dark Second Edition, running scripted co-op campaigns, monster AI and threat economy so nobody has to be the villain.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Base app is free to download with paid expansion content unlocked in-app.

verdictSummary: The software here is thin: a state machine, some card decks, a threat counter, and a monster activation table. What you are actually buying is the content, dozens of hand authored quests with branching campaign logic, tuned monster behaviour, and per-expansion encounter scripts that reference the exact tiles, minis and cards in boxes you already own. An agent can build you a very competent homebrew engine in a weekend, and it will run a dungeon crawl fine, but it will be running your dungeons, not the licensed campaigns. Rewriting those quests yourself is not a coding problem, it is a design and playtesting problem measured in months. Also worth noting the app is free to install, so you are not escaping a subscription, you are escaping a one-time expansion unlock.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that acts as automated dungeon master for your own homebrew scenarios: tracks threat, draws from an exploration deck, activates monster groups by rules you define, and saves campaign progress between sessions.
requirements: The physical board game: tiles, minis, tokens, dice, hero and monster stat cards
Your own quest and encounter content written as JSON, because the published campaigns are copyrighted
A tablet or laptop at the table, since there is no phone app unless you build one
Willingness to playtest and rebalance your own monster AI
whatYouLose: Every published campaign and expansion quest, which is the actual product
Branching campaign state that remembers your choices across ten plus sessions of authored story
Balanced monster activation logic that has been tuned against real play, not guessed at
Narrative text, art and voice that make the app feel like a game rather than a spreadsheet
Rules-accurate handling of edge cases: line of sight, fatigue, conditions, hero abilities that interact with Overlord behaviour
moatNotes: The rules are public, the campaigns are not. Anything you build has to reference components in a box the publisher controls, and republishing their quest scripts is straightforwardly infringing.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the value is authored content tied to plastic you already own. People pay for expansion unlocks so five friends can sit down and play a story someone else designed, balanced and debugged, with no one drawing the short straw and playing the antagonist. A homebrew engine solves the mechanical bookkeeping, which was never the hard part. Nobody is paying a monthly fee here anyway, so the DIY math is unusually bad: you would be spending a weekend of engineering plus months of scenario design to avoid a single small purchase.
notes: The engine is a weekend; the campaigns are not. The moat is content rights: hand authored, playtested quests welded to components only the publisher sells.
prompt:
Build a local-first "automated overlord" companion app for a tabletop dungeon crawl I run at my kitchen table.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + React + TypeScript
- Tailwind for styling
- Zustand for state, persisted to localStorage
- No backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no network calls at all
- Single page app, runs with `npm run dev`, also builds to static files I can open from a tablet on the same wifi

Content model: everything is JSON in /content, loaded at startup.
- monsters.json: name, group size, health, defense dice, attack dice, movement, abilities, activation priority rules
- scenarios.json: an ordered list of encounters, each with map notes, spawn groups, objective text, and win/lose conditions
- exploration.json: a deck of exploration cards with flavour text and effects
- campaign.json: a linear list of scenario ids plus reward text between them
Ship exactly one small example scenario I clearly own: three rooms, two monster groups, one objective. Do not include any commercial published quest content.

Core loop the app must run:
1. Pick a scenario and how many heroes are playing, scale monster group sizes from a simple table
2. Track a threat counter that ticks up each round and can be spent on reinforcements per scenario rules
3. On the overlord turn, activate each monster group in order and print plain English instructions: who moves, toward whom, what they attack, which dice to roll
4. Let me record hero positions coarsely (room + adjacency), monster damage, and conditions, since the app cannot see the board
5. Draw exploration cards when heroes open a new room
6. Detect objective completion and advance the campaign, saving state so we can stop mid session and resume next week

UI requirements: big touch targets, one primary action visible at all times, a round log I can scroll back through, and an undo for the last action because someone will always mistap.

Explicitly out of scope: line of sight math, grid level pathfinding, hero character sheets, any art assets, multiplayer sync, native mobile builds.

Finish with a README explaining the JSON schemas well enough that I can write my own scenarios without touching the code.
